title: How to Build a Product People Want to Show Other People
summary: Products can create their own distribution when customers want to share the result, ritual, identity, or experience. Learn how to design more memorable, show...
body_text: Marketing Trends for July 17th, 2026: Product Led Brand Marketing When a customer receives a surprisingly good result from a product, they take a screenshot, send it to a colleague, and explain what happened in Slack. Someone asks which tool created it. Another person requests access. By the end of the week, the product has entered three conversations the marketing team did not initiate, pay for, or observe directly. This is the distribution advantage marketers tend to overlook when separating product from brand. A useful product solves a problem. A showable product also gives the customer something worth carrying into the world: a result, an identity, a ritual, an image, a story, or an artifact that becomes easier to share than to explain. Consumer companies understand this instinctively. Packaging appears in photographs. Products become accessories. Unboxing becomes content. People display the object on desks, kitchen counters, bathroom shelves, gym bags, and social feeds because the item communicates something beyond its functional use. B2B products create social objects too. They produce reports, dashboards, benchmarks, assessments, certifications, visualizations, workflows, and results that customers can show to a manager, team, client, board, or professional community. The product does not need to become viral in the consumer-internet sense. It needs to create moments people feel motivated to repeat. Products are becoming part of the media system The boundary between product and marketing has always been porous. A beautiful object appears in a photograph. A useful template gets forwarded to a colleague. A customer wears branded merchandise because it signals membership. A product-generated report enters a quarterly meeting and becomes the company’s most persuasive sales asset. Current consumer-brand trends make this relationship unusually visible. Recent Vogue Business reporting described food, beverage, and wellness companies borrowing the visual language of fashion and beauty. Products such as premium water, protein snacks, and herbal teas are being designed as lifestyle objects that look appropriate in a creator’s feed or a carefully composed photograph. Founders interviewed for the article emphasized that product, packaging, imagery, retail, partnerships, and campaigns should feel as though they belong to the same world. The packaging does not merely contain the product. It becomes a distribution surface. McKinsey has separately identified “emotion-first products” as an emerging business model in which anticipation, identity, affinity, and community are designed into the commercial proposition from the beginning. Emotion becomes part of the economic system rather than a benefit marketing tries to add after the product is finished. That idea applies far beyond consumer goods. A B2B company may never produce a photogenic bottle. It can still build a product experience that gives users a result they want other people to see. Showability begins with a real product truth A shareable moment cannot be sustained through decoration alone. A visually distinctive product may earn an initial post. A surprising campaign may generate curiosity. Customers continue sharing when the product gives them something meaningful: a better result, an easier routine, a useful insight, a sense of progress, or a way to express who they are. The recent interest in design-led consumer products carries an important caveat. Aesthetic packaging can increase desire, but the product still has to justify repeat use. The wellness and supplement categories are increasingly crowded with visually sophisticated brands, while consumers are also asking harder questions about efficacy, convenience, scientific support, and actual product performance. Marketing teams should therefore begin with the truth the product can reliably create. For Surface, that truth might be the moment a marketing or sales team sees the complete history behind a lead rather than receiving a form submission without context. A rep who can see which articles, case studies, integrations, and pricing pages a buyer reviewed receives something immediately useful and demonstrable. The full lead journey is both a capability and an artifact. It gives the user information they can bring into a sales conversation, team review, or performance report. The product creates something that is easier to show than a generic claim about “better marketing intelligence.” The five kinds of product moments people share Products become showable in several different ways. Companies should decide which type fits the customer and use case rather than forcing every product into a social-media loop. The result Customers share an outcome they are proud of. This may be revenue growth, time saved, an improved conversion rate, a finished design, a solved technical problem, a cleaner forecast, or a personal transformation. The product gives the customer a before-and-after story. Results travel when they are specific, credible, and easy to communicate. A statement such as “we improved efficiency” contains little social value. A report showing that a team reduced lead-response time from four hours to forty seconds gives the customer a concrete achievement to present. The artifact The product produces something that can leave the interface. Examples include a benchmark report, visual analysis, certificate, scorecard, strategy map, generated image, presentation, project plan, audit, or customer-facing deliverable. The artifact should preserve enough product identity to create attribution without becoming an advertisement. A useful report that subtly identifies the system which produced it can travel naturally. A report covered in promotional banners makes the customer feel as though they are distributing company collateral. The ritual The product becomes part of a repeated behavior. Morning fitness summaries, annual listening reports, weekly team scorecards, project retrospectives, and monthly business reviews all create recurring opportunities for customers to discuss the product. Rituals help brands accumulate meaning. A one-time campaign asks people to remember. A repeated product behavior gives them another reason to encounter and use the brand. The identity signal The product communicates something about the user. A person may share a tool because it makes them appear informed, creative, efficient, discerning, technically capable, environmentally conscious, or part of a particular community. Identity can be subtle. A developer sharing an elegant technical workflow signals expertise. A marketing leader distributing a clear attribution framework signals operational sophistication. The product helps the customer tell a story about themselves. The discovery The product reveals something the customer did not know. Unexpected insights are naturally conversational. A user shares the finding because it changes an assumption, exposes an opportunity, or gives the team language for a problem it had previously struggled to describe. Products with analytics, research, classification, or recommendation features are especially capable of creating discovery moments. The interface should make the insight clear enough that users can understand and explain it without reconstructing the analysis manually. Consumer products turn use into culture The strongest consumer examples show how utility, design, ritual, and community reinforce each other. Vaseline offers an unusual case because its core product is more than 150 years old. Unilever CMO Leandro Barreto recently described how creators and customers have expanded the cultural life of the product by demonstrating unconventional uses, including applying it to dog noses or using it inside shoes. The company gained relevance by observing and embracing how communities were reinterpreting a familiar object. The marketing did not invent every use from headquarters. Customers created material around the product because its flexibility invited experimentation. This suggests a different approach to product-led marketing. The company does not need to control every interpretation. It needs to provide enough product integrity, recognizability, and openness for customers to discover uses worth discussing. Marketing teams can then document, organize, validate, and amplify the most useful behavior. Customer creativity becomes research as well as distribution. B2B products need shareable outcomes, not consumer gimmicks B2B teams often misunderstand product virality by copying visible consumer mechanics. They add badges, celebration animations, social-sharing buttons, points, leaderboards, and decorative summaries without asking whether the customer gains anything by sharing them. The mechanism exists. The motivation does not. A professional user usually shares a product output because it helps them perform their role. They may want to: Demonstrate progress to a manager Explain a decision to another department Give a client a useful deliverable Build consensus around a strategy Prove that an investment worked Warn the team about a risk Establish personal credibility Teach colleagues a better process Compare performance against a benchmark Request additional budget or support The showable B2B product should make one of those jobs easier. A marketing dashboard becomes shareable when it clearly explains what changed and what the team should do next. A security report becomes shareable when it helps an executive understand risk. A lead-operations product becomes shareable when sales can see why a prospect was prioritized and what the buyer researched before converting. Surface’s broader content marketing operating model separates visibility, trust, conversion, distribution, and measurement. Product-generated artifacts can connect all five. They provide useful material, demonstrate the company’s method, travel between people, and create a path toward commercial action. Design the handoff between product and conversation The shareable moment usually occurs at a boundary. A user finishes a task and needs approval. A marketer discovers a trend and needs to inform leadership. A sales representative receives a lead and needs to prepare for outreach. A customer completes an assessment and needs to discuss the result. Products should identify these boundaries and make the handoff easier. Ask: What has the user just accomplished? Who needs to see the result next? What context will that person require? Which format makes the information easiest to understand? What portion can be shared safely? How should the recipient return to the product? What product or brand identity should remain attached? The answers may lead to exportable reports, collaborative links, presentations, email summaries, CRM records, annotated screenshots, public profiles, embeddable modules, or client-ready PDFs. A “share” button is the final interface element. The product strategy begins with understanding why the user would press it. Make the product legible in ten seconds Showable products create clear stories. The customer should be able to point to the output and say: Here is what changed. Here is what the product discovered. Here is why the result matters. Here is what we should do next. Dense interfaces may contain important detail, but the first layer needs a legible conclusion. Surface’s storytelling work applies inside the product as much as it applies to campaigns. Hierarchy, tension, evidence, sequence, and explanation determine whether a user can turn data into a story. This is especially important for AI-generated results. A product that produces an answer without visible reasoning, sources, caveats, or next steps may create temporary surprise. A product that helps the user understand and defend the result creates an artifact they can use with confidence. Let the customer receive the social value Companies often overbrand the shareable output. They place a giant logo above a small customer result. They force recipients through an acquisition form. They require public posting. They make the user’s achievement feel like an advertisement for the vendor. The better question is who should look impressive. In most cases, the customer should. The report should help the customer appear informed. The visualization should help them communicate clearly. The assessment should help them lead a better conversation. The benchmark should give them useful context. Product attribution can remain visible without consuming the artifact. This approach creates a healthier exchange. The customer receives professional or personal value. The company receives distribution and association with the value created. Build a recognizable product world Showability becomes more powerful when the product, brand, content, and campaigns feel connected. The recent design-led CPG trend is useful because those companies are building coherent worlds. The product, packaging, photography, retail environment, creator partnerships, and storytelling share a recognizable logic. B2B companies can create the same coherence without copying consumer aesthetics. A product-generated report can use the same terminology as the company’s research. A dashboard can reflect the hierarchy used in sales conversations. A customer assessment can connect to educational content. A benchmark can become an annual editorial asset. A product insight can become the starting point for an executive discussion or customer story. The product then participates in the brand instead of sitting behind the marketing layer as a separate visual and linguistic system. Teams using AI without losing their brand voice should apply the same discipline to generated product outputs. Default AI language can make every insight sound as though it came from the same anonymous consultant. Product voice should remain clear, useful, and recognizable. Measure whether customers carry the product forward Product-led brand effects can be measured, although the evidence will be distributed. Useful signals include: Export and share rates Collaborative invitations Public links created Screenshots or product images mentioned online Referral traffic from shared artifacts New users entering through collaboration Repeat use of reports and assessments Customer references during sales conversations Branded search following major product moments Template or artifact reuse Creator and community adoption Lead quality from shared-product journeys Retention among users who share or collaborate Teams should also review the qualitative evidence. Why did someone share? Who received it? What did the artifact help the user accomplish? Which part of the product did the recipient remember? Lead journey tracking can reveal what happens when a recipient enters the owned experience. The company can see whether shared-product visitors inspect use cases, read comparisons, view pricing, and eventually convert. The objective is not to claim that every share caused revenue. It is to understand whether the product is creating its own useful paths into the market. A practical product-showability workshop Bring together product, marketing, customer success, design, and sales. Choose one high-value customer workflow and answer the following questions. What does the customer accomplish? Describe the outcome in the customer’s language rather than the product’s feature vocabulary. Who needs to see it? Identify the colleague, manager, client, community, or external stakeholder who benefits from the result. Why would the customer share? Define the professional, emotional, or social value the customer receives. What should travel? Choose the result, evidence, context, and next action the recipient needs. What should remain attached? Preserve appropriate product identity, source information, methodology, and a route back into the experience. What could create discomfort? Review privacy, confidentiality, competitive sensitivity, personal data, and the risk of accidental disclosure. How will the company learn? Track use, ask customers about the behavior, and use the findings to improve the product and marketing system. The exercise should produce a real feature or workflow hypothesis. “Make it more viral” is not a product requirement. The product should give marketing something true to amplify Marketing teams often search for a story while the product experience remains generic. They develop campaign concepts, commission research, hire creators, and build visual systems because the product itself provides few distinctive moments. Those efforts can still create value. They become considerably stronger when the product gives them something real. A powerful result, elegant ritual, recognizable artifact, unexpected discovery, or customer-created use case gives marketing durable material. The team can explain it, document it, distribute it, and connect it to a larger point of view. The company no longer has to ask customers to believe that the product is interesting. Customers are already showing one another why.

title: High Roller Technologies Appoints Thomas Scaria as Chief Product Officer
summary: View High Roller Technologies' press releases. Stay informed on their online gambling tech innovations and business updates by signing up to their emails.
body_text: High Roller Technologies Appoints Thomas Scaria as Chief Product Officer August 12, 2026 8:00 am EDT Download as PDF Product and financial markets executive to lead ROLR prediction markets platform development, launch execution and global product strategy LAS VEGAS, Nevada, Aug. 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- High Roller Technologies, Inc. (“High Roller” or the “Company”) (NYSE: ROLR), a publicly traded online gaming and prediction markets company, today announced the appointment of Thomas Scaria, CFA, to the newly created position of Chief Product Officer, reporting to CEO Seth Young. The creation of the Chief Product Officer position further expands High Roller’s leadership and product-development capabilities as the Company prepares to launch ROLR prediction markets and continues to invest in its broader portfolio of real-money consumer products. “Thomas brings a rare combination of product leadership, financial markets expertise, technical understanding, and entrepreneurial experience that is highly relevant to the next phase of High Roller’s growth,” said Seth Young, Chief Executive Officer of High Roller Technologies. “As we advance toward the launch of the ROLR prediction markets platform domestically and internationally, disciplined product strategy and execution will be critical. The creation of the Chief Product Officer position reflects that priority, and we are pleased to welcome Thomas to our leadership team.” “I’m excited to join High Roller,” said Scaria. “Prediction markets are the expression of a market in its most primitive form: one clear real-world outcome you can take a view on. You don’t need to learn the underlying complexity associated with other derivatives like options, swaps and futures. The removal of that educational barrier is why prediction markets have exploded into mainstream culture. ROLR sits on established, federally regulated U.S. derivatives infrastructure, and we’re focused on turning that foundation into novel consumer experiences that expand the category.” Scaria will lead the Company’s product vision, strategy, roadmap, and execution across its prediction markets business. His responsibilities include overseeing the development and optimization of the ROLR prediction markets platform, and working across technology, compliance, operations, marketing, and commercial partnerships to deliver intuitive, engaging, and scalable customer experiences. About Thomas Scaria Scaria brings more than a decade of experience spanning product development, financial services, digital assets, payments, trading, market structure and go-to-market strategy. He was most recently Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Lore, a blockchain-based asset management platform. Under his leadership, Lore raised approximately $7.5 million from prominent digital-asset investors including Polychain Capital and Multicoin Capital. Lore served over 100,000 customers, including 1,500 online fund managers who managed over $50 million in assets on its proprietary, internet-first custody and fund management infrastructure. Before Lore, Scaria was an Entrepreneur in Residence at Polychain Capital, where he launched an early social trading network on Ethereum that was used by over 15% of the blockchain’s retail traders by mid-2021. Prior to his entrepreneurial work, Scaria led the expansion of Wyre, a B2B cross-border payments platform, into the emergent decentralized finance (DeFi) category, having joined Wyre to lead its over-the-counter trading business. He built that trading background at Citi as a Senior Investment Associate, structuring and selling bespoke derivatives to the bank’s institutional and family-office clients. Scaria is a CFA charterholder and holds a B.S. in Biomedical Engineering from the University of Southern California. About High Roller Technologies, Inc. High Roller Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: ROLR) is a publicly traded online gaming and prediction markets company, known for its innovative casino brands High Roller and Fruta , and its prediction markets brand, ROLR . The Company delivers cutting-edge real-money consumer facing products that are intuitive and user-friendly. With a diverse portfolio of over 6,000 premium online casino games from more than 90 leading game providers, High Roller Technologies offers an immersive and engaging gaming experience in the rapidly expanding multi-billion-dollar iGaming industry. As an award-winning operator, High Roller Technologies continues to redefine the future of market engagement through innovation, performance, and a commitment to excellence. For more information, please visit the Company’s investor relations website and follow High Roller Technologies on X , Facebook , and LinkedIn . title: The Best Cheap Fast Cars of 2026
summary: You don’t need to spend a lot to get a fast car. Surprisingly, some of the more budget-friendly options also happen to provide the most enjoyable driving experiences. Here are our top new car picks.
body_text: Shopping for a car that's genuinely fun to drive doesn't have to mean emptying your bank account. The market for cheap fast cars is built on the idea that thrilling performance and everyday practicality can coexist at an affordable price point. These vehicles offer a welcome dose of excitement for the daily commute or a weekend drive on a winding road, providing more powerful engines, sharper handling, and a more engaging experience than a standard commuter car, but without the six-figure price tag of a high-end sports car. This guide highlights a range of options that deliver speed and enjoyment without sacrificing usability. Whether you're drawn to the classic muscle of a Ford Mustang, the all-wheel-drive (AWD) grip of a Subaru WRX, or the balanced performance of a hot hatchback like the Volkswagen Golf GTI, there's a budget-friendly performance car to fit your needs. We'll explore what makes each car quick, how it handles daily tasks like hauling groceries, and what you can expect to pay, helping you find the right blend of speed, practicality, and value. What Makes CarGurus Best Cars Guides Different The Best Cheap Fast Cars Ford Mustang Honda Civic Si Subaru WRX BMW 2 Series Hyundai Elantra N Mazda MX-5 Miata Volkswagen Golf GTI Subaru BRZ Volkswagen Jetta GLI Toyota GR Corolla FAQs Shopping Tools Related Topics 1. Ford Mustang CarGurus expert rating: 7.2 out of 10 CarGurus user rating: 4.6 out of 5 Percentage of Good and Great Deals available on CarGurus: 29.1% Overall CarGurus rating: 4.5 out of 5 Pros Cons Powerful engine Cramped back seat Great handling Not much cargo space Excellent value for money Noisy If you want real straight-line speed without supercar money, the Ford Mustang is one of the simplest ways to get there. The base 2.3-liter turbo EcoBoost makes 315 hp and 350 lb-ft of torque, and it's paired with a 10-speed automatic driving the rear wheels; that combination should be quick enough for most shoppers looking for a cheap fast car, with an estimated zero-to-60-mph time of about 5 seconds. For buyers chasing the classic muscle-car hit, the Mustang GT's 5.0-liter V8 brings 480 hp and 415 lb-ft of torque (or 486 hp and 418 lb-ft with the optional Active Exhaust), plus an available manual transmission with rev matching that's easy to drive day to day. The Mustang also backs up the speed with livability upgrades that matter if this is your daily driver: a modernized cabin with a large 13.2-inch touchscreen and digital gauge cluster, plus standard Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. Space is a reminder that this is still a coupe/convertible first—rear seats are tight, and cargo room tops out at 13.3 cubic feet in the Fastback (10.3 cubic feet in the Convertible)—but it's enough for a weekend trip. Standard driver-assistance features like automatic emergency braking, lane-keep assist, blind-spot monitoring with rear cross-traffic alert, and rear parking sensors add peace of mind, and the pricing keeps it in budget territory for the performance. The CarGurus Verdict: "The Ford Mustang returns for a final tour as its primary rivals head to retirement. This seventh-generation pony car is based on its predecessor but receives numerous upgrades that significantly improve its interior and technology. For fun on a budget, it's difficult to beat a Mustang, and this newest version continues the tradition with a healthy dose of nostalgia." - Mark Takahashi Read our most recent Ford Mustang review Search for Ford Mustang See all 2011 Ford Mustang $20,094 66,607 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Pleasant Valley, IA 2017 Ford Mustang $25,894 60,839 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Charlotte, NC 2020 Ford Mustang $35,427 24,994 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Draper, UT 2019 Ford Mustang $41,344 19,278 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Oklahoma City, OK 2017 Ford Mustang $19,343 38,199 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Fredonia, NY 2021 Ford Mustang $34,250 40,274 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Albany, NY 2. Honda Civic Si CarGurus expert rating: 6.8 out of 10 CarGurus user rating: 4.5 out of 5 Percentage of Good and Great Deals available on CarGurus: 28.7% Overall CarGurus rating: 4.5 out of 5 Pros Cons Choice of body styles All-wheel drive not available Enjoyable to drive Noisy at speed Premium interior materials Outdated technology The Honda Civic's appeal depends heavily on which version you choose. The Civic Sport sedan we last tested uses a 2.0-liter four-cylinder rated at 150 hp and 133 lb-ft of torque, routed through a continuously variable transmission (CVT) to the front wheels, and it can feel underpowered when merging or passing. That said, the payoff is in how confidently it carries speed through corners: precise steering, a well-tuned strut/multi-link suspension, and strong four-wheel-disc brakes make it genuinely fun on a twisty road, even if straight-line punch isn't the point. If your budget can stretch, the hybrid powertrain is called out for delivering "remarkable power and impressive efficiency," which is the smarter route for shoppers prioritizing quickness without giving up mpg. Daily usability is a big part of the Civic's value equation. The cabin looks and feels a step above many compact cars thanks to thoughtful materials and excellent, "normal" ergonomics, but the standard 7-inch tech can feel dated, and Apple CarPlay/Android Auto require a cable. The sedan's 14.8 cubic feet of trunk space is a real plus, and the available safety tech is strong: every Civic gets Honda Sensing, and the sedan earns a five-star overall National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) rating, though some driver-assist behaviors (like adaptive cruise control braking) can be irritating. Pricing runs from $25,790 to $34,690 including destination for most trims, and with 31.9% of listings marked as Good or Great Deals on CarGurus, it's worth watching the market closely if you want Civic handling while keeping your "cheap fast" budget under control. The CarGurus Verdict: "You'll pay a premium to buy a Honda Civic. In many ways, it's worth the extra money. In others, not so much. Still, while there are better deals in the compact car class, few are as satisfying to drive, and that's true even when the Civic is equipped with its base engine." - Christian Wardlaw Read our most recent Honda Civic review Search for Honda Civic See all 2017 Honda Civic $17,349 57,132 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Fargo, ND 2020 Honda Civic $19,897 74,115 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Hutchinson, KS 2015 Honda Civic $9,798 127,796 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Grand Junction, CO 2018 Honda Civic $13,994 150,338 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Twin Falls, ID 2018 Honda Civic $17,090 88,710 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Livingston, MT 2017 Honda Civic $8,584 183,000 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Clearfield, UT 3. Subaru WRX CarGurus expert rating: 7.7 out of 10 CarGurus user rating: 4.8 out of 5 Percentage of Good and Great Deals available on CarGurus: 30.7% Overall CarGurus rating: 4.5 out of 5 Pros Cons Stylish design Unintuitive technology Great handling Poor value for money Manual transmission available Less cargo space than rivals If you want a cheap fast car that can still pull daily-driver duty year-round, the Subaru WRX leans into its rally roots with standard AWD and a 2.4-liter turbocharged four-cylinder boxer making 271 hp and 258 lb-ft of torque. A six-speed manual is standard, while Subaru's optional CVT (the Subaru Performance Transmission) tries to mimic a traditional automatic with simulated shifts; either way, the WRX's grip and confidence on a back road are a big part of the appeal, especially with standard summer tires. It's also a grown-up WRX in day-to-day driving—quiet and comfortable enough for commuting—though the on-road character can feel a bit "muted" compared with earlier versions. Affordability is where shoppers need to be picky about trims: pricing climbs quickly as you move up the lineup. Fuel economy is respectable for a performance sedan—up to 22 miles per gallon (MPG) combined with the manual (21 MPG combined with the CVT)—but Subaru recommends 93-octane fuel, which can nudge running costs upward if you drive it hard. Practicality is decent for a sporty compact sedan, but the 12.5-cubic-foot trunk trails rivals, and the cabin has an odd everyday miss: There's no truly good place to set a modern smartphone near the USB ports. On the plus side, outward visibility is excellent, and available EyeSight driver-assistance (offered with the CVT only) plus strong crash-test results from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) make the WRX easier to live with when "fast" also has to mean "safe." Every 2025 Gran Coupe comes standard with AWD and a seven-speed dual-clutch automatic, and BMW claims zero-to-60-mph runs of 6 seconds for the 228 xDrive and 4.5 seconds for the quicker M235 xDrive we drove. Adaptive dampers are standard across the lineup, so you can toggle between softer and firmer responses, though the M235 with the M Performance package leans noticeably firm and can send more jostling into the cabin over rougher seams. As a daily driver, the 2 Series Gran Coupe does a solid job balancing speed with real-world usability: The front sport seats are supportive without being difficult to slide into, and the trunk is rated at 12 cubic feet (and feels bigger than the number suggests for luggage and errands). Tech highlights include a standard 10.7-inch touchscreen with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, a wireless charging pad, and Harman Kardon audio, but some common adjustments—like changing adaptive cruise control following distance—require extra menu digging. title: Flotek Industries Provides Update on Puerto Rico Power Project and Reaffirms its Full-Year 2026 Guidance
summary: Flotek Industries, Inc. ("Flotek" or the "Company") (NYSE: FTK) today provided an update regarding its previously announced participation in the Emergency Temporary Power Generation Puerto Rico...
body_text: Press Releases Overview Stock Information Stock Quote & Chart Investment Calculator Historical Stock Price SEC Filings Governance Executive Management Board of Directors Board Committees Governance Documents Compliance Hotline News & Events Press Releases Events Presentations Flotek Industries Provides Update on Puerto Rico Power Project and Reaffirms its Full-Year 2026 Guidance Open a printable version of this page Email the URL of this page to a friend Get the RSS feed for this page Download a PDF version of this page Share this page on Twitter Share this page on LinkedIn Share this page on Facebook HOUSTON , Aug. 18, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- Flotek Industries, Inc. ("Flotek" or the "Company") (NYSE: FTK) today provided an update regarding its previously announced participation in the Emergency Temporary Power Generation Puerto Rico project ("PREPA Contract"). This update does not change the Company's previously issued 2026 financial guidance, which did not include any potential contribution from the PREPA Contract. As previously disclosed, on August 4, 2026, the Company raised its full-year 2026 financial guidance following record second-quarter performance. The updated outlook targets total revenue of $340 million to $350 million and Adjusted EBITDA(1) of $47 million to $51 million, excluding any potential contributions from the PREPA Contract. As previously disclosed on August 3, 2026, Flotek entered into a 10-year agreement to provide power-generation equipment and its proprietary PWRtek gas-conditioning, distribution and real-time monitoring systems in support of the proposed 400-megawatt project at the Aguirre Power Plant. The Company has filed a Current Report on Form 8-K today with the Securities and Exchange Commission providing a factual update on the current status of the PREPA Contract in light of the developments further discussed below. Flotek joined the project after the original procurement and execution of the PREPA Contract between the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority ("PREPA") and the initially selected consortium. Before Flotek assumed its defined project responsibilities, the Company was advised that questions regarding the authorization of certain signatures associated with the PREPA Contract had been raised and had been fully vetted through the procurement process. PREPA and the Third-Party Procurement Office subsequently reviewed Flotek's qualifications, approved its participation and authorized the substitution through which Flotek assumed the applicable project responsibilities on July 31, 2026. The Financial Oversight and Management Board for Puerto Rico (the "Oversight Board") has announced that its members have voted to direct PREPA to terminate the PREPA Contract. On August 17, 2026, PREPA issued a directive to all consortium parties, including the Company, to immediately hold all work related to the development of the project pending PREPA's evaluation of these developments. In addition, on August 17, 2026, a firm with an admitted short interest position in the Company published a report making allegations about the Company's business that we believe was intended to drive down the market price of the Company's common stock. As of the date of this release, PREPA has not delivered a formal notice of termination of the PREPA Contract to the Company. The timing and ultimate scope of Flotek's participation remain subject to resolution of the PREPA Contract matter, satisfaction of applicable contractual conditions, financing and bonding requirements, governmental and regulatory approvals, and the project proceeding to deployment. No assurance can be given that the project will proceed as originally contemplated, that the work stoppage will be lifted, that the Oversight Board's revocation will be reversed or modified, or that the Company will realize any or all of the expected revenues under the PREPA Contract. We are unable to reconcile this forward-looking non-GAAP financial measure to the most directly comparable GAAP financial measure without unreasonable efforts, as we are unable to predict with a reasonable degree of certainty the impact of certain items that would be expected to impact the GAAP financial measure, including, among other items, certain stock-based compensation costs and interest costs related to fluctuations in borrowings under the Company's asset based loan. These items do not impact the non-GAAP financial measure. Guidance does not add back non-cash amortization of contract assets estimated to total approximately $9 million during full-year 2026. About Flotek Industries, Inc. Flotek Industries, Inc. is a leading chemistry and data technology company focused on servicing the Energy industry. The Company's technologies leverage near real-time data to deliver innovative solutions to maximize customer returns. Flotek has an intellectual property portfolio of over 130 patents, over 20 years of field and laboratory data, and a global presence in more than 59 countries. Flotek has established collaborative partnerships focused on sustainable and optimized chemistry and data solutions, aiming to reduce the environmental impact of energy on land, air, water and people. Flotek is based in Houston, Texas and its common shares are traded on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol "FTK." For additional information, please visit www.flotekind.com . Readers are cautioned not to place undue reliance on these forward-looking statements, which speak only as of the date made. title: The Future of Recruitment: What Comes Next for Frontline Hiring
summary: Recruiting software is becoming a system that acts, not one that reports. What that shift means for frontline hiring, and how to tell if you're ready.
body_text: For frontline employers, the future of recruitment is hiring software that finishes work across the hiring process, not software that reports on it. A May 2025 Gartner survey found that 82% of HR leaders plan to implement some form of agentic AI. Yet in Aptitude Research’s early-2026 frontline analysis, only 25% of talent acquisition leaders call their current technology very effective at high-volume hiring. The AI being sold into recruiting far outruns the hiring work it finishes. A stalled screening or scheduling queue can leave a frontline shift uncovered within days, so employers need software that moves candidates through the administrative stages without waiting on a recruiter at every step. It runs screening, scheduling, outreach, and document collection under employer-defined rules, while managers review the consequential decisions: offers, accommodations, appeals, and exceptions. What does the future of recruitment mean for frontline hiring? For frontline hiring, the shift is in what the software does: it moves from recording and reporting hiring work to running it. Three different technologies get bundled under that promise, and telling them apart is the first job of anyone evaluating vendors this year. Trigger-based automation fires one predefined action per event: a confirmation text when an application arrives, or a review routing when a knockout question fails. Scoring and recommendation systems rank candidates against role requirements and tell a recruiter who to call next. Agentic systems go further: they pursue a hiring outcome across multiple steps, screening applicants and booking interviews inside the employer’s permissions and approval rules, and move candidates between stages while routing consequential decisions to a person, which is what separates an agentic applicant tracking system (ATS) from a traditional system of record. As HRCI Chief Business Officer Andre Allen distinguishes the three , “Predictive AI shows us what might happen, generative AI creates something new, but agentic AI takes the next step: acting on our behalf.” What is not changing: the manager still owns the offer, the exception, and the judgment call, and a candidate still has to show up on Day 1 and be worth keeping three months later. Agentic systems take the queue work between application and offer; accountability for the hire stays with the manager. What’s changing in how frontline roles get filled Across every stage of the frontline funnel, software now executes the administrative work, which is most of how AI is already changing hourly hiring . Screening and qualification begin the moment an application arrives: knockout questions and availability matching finish in minutes with a score attached, instead of sitting in a recruiter’s queue overnight. Candidates who meet the documented criteria pick an interview slot from a synced calendar before the impulse to apply fades, and the phone tag that used to burn days disappears. Outreach runs continuously: stalled applicants get nudged, and past workers hear from you before peak season instead of you paying to source strangers. Compliance steps become workflow stages rather than follow-up tasks, so a missing document surfaces before Day 1, not after. For frontline roles, skills-based hiring means fast, accurate verification of the credentials and availability that decide whether someone can do the job. In trucking, employers verify commercial driver’s license (CDL) class and current medical certification, then check the federally mandated employment history. In healthcare it means licensure confirmed at the primary source; in retail and quick-service restaurants (QSR) it mostly comes down to availability that matches the shifts you need covered. Want to See What Agentic AI Can Do for Your Team? Download the Free Guide: Agentic AI for Frontline Hiring & Retention Explore how top HR teams are using agentic AI to speed up hiring, improve onboarding, and reduce frontline turnover—at scale. This guide breaks down real-world use cases, ROI benchmarks, and a 90-day roadmap for getting started. Download Now On July 1, 2025, the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) Clearinghouse listed 190,402 CDL and permit holders in prohibited status. Run that check as an automated stage on application arrival, and the result and its timestamp land in the candidate record, where an auditor can find them. Why frontline hiring is where these shifts land first Frontline hiring is the proving ground because software failure becomes operational failure in the same week. Volume is high, decision windows run in hours, and the hiring rules vary by city and state across every location in your footprint. Most candidates apply from their phones, and the employer who makes a concrete offer first usually wins them. With fewer applicants per opening, every candidate lost to a slow stage costs more as openings grow. Turnover then keeps refilling the same roles: a location that refills the same job twice in a year pays the recruiting, onboarding, and ramp cost twice, before any of it shows up as an uncovered shift. What candidates will expect from the hiring process Frontline candidates expect a fast, mobile-first process that is transparent about pay and shift and clear about when AI is evaluating them. Put the pay range, shift details, and an AI-use notice on the first mobile screen, and a candidate can decide before investing time instead of discovering the terms late. Candidate experience used to be a branding project; now a slow or confusing application limits how many candidates reach the next stage, and a slow reply hands them to whoever answers first. Shift transparency is becoming a legal obligation too: predictive scheduling laws in cities and states including Chicago, New York City, Seattle, San Francisco, Philadelphia, and Oregon generally require posting schedules at least 14 days in advance . The process also has to survive a phone-width read: frontline candidates apply between shifts and abandon anything that demands a desktop or drags past a few minutes. The assumption that these candidates resist AI does not hold up. The Frontline Report 2025, which Fountain produced with Lighthouse Research & Advisory from a survey of nearly 2,000 frontline workers, found that 74% said they would rather deal with AI during hiring than with traditional methods. What they reject is being evaluated by AI without being told. Disclosing AI use at the first step, before a candidate invests time, is what separates acceptance from a walk-off. What stays human, and where oversight sits Humans keep offers, exceptions, accommodations, appeals, and any decision your team would have to defend in an audit. Document which administrative stages run automatically and which decisions require manager approval, and each review and override is recorded as it happens rather than reconstructed after an audit request. Defined permissions and audit logs are what make agentic hiring work, not model size or demo quality, and teams have to redesign workflows before they deploy. A Gartner forecast on agentic AI project cancellations predicts that more than 40% will be scrapped by the end of 2027, over escalating costs, unclear value, or inadequate risk controls. Effective deployments are built on those controls even when a demo never shows them. State and local regulators are also setting specific expectations around automated hiring decisions. Under New York City’s Local Law 144 , in force since 2023, employers that use an automated employment decision tool are generally required to obtain a bias audit no more than a year old and to give candidates at least 10 business days’ notice. California’s Civil Rights Council regulations , effective October 1, 2025, clarify that using an automated-decision system that produces an unlawful disparate impact can violate state employment law. When those verification and human-review steps live inside the workflow, the record is captured as the work happens, not reconstructed after the audit letter arrives. Treat this as general orientation, not legal advice; confirm your obligations with counsel. How to tell whether your hiring operation is ready Start where your team still translates insight into action by hand. Map those stages for one role and one location: when the dashboard shows drop-off at the scheduling step and a coordinator spends Tuesday clearing it, that is the handoff to automate. Check five conditions before you deploy: Clean operational data: Keep location lists, role requirements, availability rules, and pay bands current enough that the system can act on them without a person interpreting them first. Clear permissions and approval thresholds: Document which administrative actions run autonomously, which decisions need a manager’s sign-off, and where the workflow escalates. Integration with your systems of record: Make sure hires, hours, and compliance records flow into your human capital management (HCM) system without creating a second system of record. Willingness to redesign the workflow: Fix the broken process before you add software to it, or the system will just automate the breakage. Measurement that would show a change: Track time-to-hire, drop-off by stage and device, Day 1 show rate, first-90-day retention, and cost per hire at the location level. An operation that clears all five is ready to let software execute. One that does not will spend its pilot cleaning data. How Fountain runs the future of frontline hiring Fountain is Frontline Superintelligence: connected software that runs workflows across sourcing, screening, onboarding, and scheduling instead of reporting on them. Cue , the orchestration layer inside every Fountain product, takes a plain-English goal and builds the workflows that carry it out, then keeps them running. A multi-unit restaurant operator can type, “We’re opening 12 locations across Texas before summer: build the hiring plan, sourcing, screening, and I-9 steps for each store,” and Cue configures each one. Cue coordinates the agents that handle the recurring work, so the screen, the interview slot, and the new-hire paperwork stop being separate queues that each wait on a person to restart them. Anna , the AI Recruiter, runs phone and text screens around the clock and surfaces scores for the hiring team’s final call. Emma , AI 24/7 Support, answers the candidate and paperwork questions that otherwise stall a start date. Sam , AI Satisfaction, checks in after Day 1 and flags retention risk early. Managers review the consequential decisions and approve every offer and exception. Those agents act on one connected platform, because payroll, tax, and audit obligations still live in the HCM. Fountain connects its ATS , Sourcing , CRM , Onboarding , and Shift & Scheduling to UKG, SAP, ADP, and Workday through the Integration Center , so new-hire records, hours, and verification documents land in the existing system of record as the work happens. That keeps one record instead of a second store of decisions to reconcile when a bias audit asks who signed off on which output. With Fountain, Alto reported hiring 450 drivers in 6 months by 3 recruiters at a $300 cost per hire, with a 2- to 7-day time-to-offer, compared with the $4,700 average cost per hire cited by SHRM. An uncovered shift can’t wait in a follow-up queue, which is why the frontline is where recruiting software that runs the work pulls ahead of software that only reports it. Fountain was named a Niche Player in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Talent Acquisition Suites. See it against one of your own high-volume roles: Book a demo to watch Cue configure a location’s hiring workflow, Anna screen a candidate by voice, and a manager approve the offer. Frequently asked questions about the future of recruitment Will AI replace recruiters and hiring managers? No. Agentic systems remove the screening-queue work and surface results for the hiring team, handle candidate self-scheduling, and collect documents before Day 1, but a person still owns the offer and any exception or accommodation. Rules in New York City, Illinois, and California point the same way: toward notice, bias audits, and documented human review around automated decisions. What laws regulate AI in hiring in the US right now? New York City’s Local Law 144 has required bias audits and candidate notice since 2023. Illinois HB 3773 took effect January 1, 2026, and California’s Civil Rights Council regulations took effect October 1, 2025. Multi-state frontline employers face a patchwork that rewards centralized documentation. How is frontline recruiting different from corporate recruiting? Frontline recruiting runs on volume and speed, and the gating checks are verification rather than resume review. Employers process thousands of mobile applications for roles where licensure, certifications, and shift availability decide who qualifies, and an unfilled role shows up as an uncovered shift rather than a delayed project.

title: USAJOBS Now Caps Federal Resumes at 2 Pages (2025 Rule): What Changed and How to Fit It
summary: As of Sept 27, 2025, USAJOBS caps federal resumes at two pages, over the limit means ineligible. Here is what changed and how to condense without losing detail.
body_text: Does USAJOBS really cap federal resumes at two pages now? Yes. As of September 27, 2025, USAJOBS holds resumes to two pages, and the limit reaches your profile resume, uploaded files, builder resumes, and searchable resumes in the Agency Talent Portal. Go over and you're out of the running for that job, not trimmed to fit. The federal content still has to be there though, so the real work is condensing decades of detail into two pages without dropping the fields that qualify you. Read your job announcement first. It spells out the requirement and any exception. The rule that flipped twenty years of federal-resume advice For most of your working life, one piece of resume advice sat outside the "keep it short" gospel: the federal resume. Everywhere else you fought to hit one page. On USAJOBS you did the opposite. You wrote long, you wrote everything, and you were told the longer and more keyword-dense the better. Five pages was ordinary, eight raised no eyebrows, and people in scientific and technical series ran fifteen pages while nobody blinked. That is over. Since September 27, 2025, USAJOBS restricts resumes to two pages. If you built your federal-resume habits any time in the last two decades, almost everything you learned about length now works against you. The reflex to pad, to prove twelve months of specialized experience with a wall of bullets, to list every duty you have ever performed since 2004, is the reflex that gets you screened out today. Here's the part that trips people up. The cap did not make the federal resume shorter in the way a private-sector one is short. It kept every content requirement that made federal resumes long in the first place and then told you to fit all of it into two pages. So the skill you need now is harder than either writing a sprawling federal resume or writing a tidy corporate one. You have to compress without gutting. What actually changed on September 27, 2025 The change is narrow and specific, which is why it catches people off guard. It is not a suggestion buried in a formatting guide. It is a technical limit wired into the system. As of that date, the two-page limit applies to your resume in every place USAJOBS stores or reads one: the resume saved in your job-seeker profile, any new resume you upload, a resume you make in the USAJOBS resume builder, and searchable resumes in the Agency Talent Portal, the pool recruiters mine for candidates. If you had a searchable resume sitting in that pool, it came out on September 27 and stays out until you post a two-page version back. Reach matters here. A lot of applicants keep one long master resume in their profile and forget it exists between job hunts. That old resume is now a liability. The cap is not something you meet once at the moment you click apply. It is a standard your stored profile has to satisfy too. The limit covers competitive-service and excepted-service announcements under Title 5, internal and external. That is the vast majority of what you see posted on USAJOBS. There are edges, which I'll get to, but assume the rule applies unless a specific announcement tells you otherwise. Why this one isn't advice. It's a gate Plenty of resume "rules" are really preferences. A recruiter would rather you keep it to a page, but a good third page won't sink you. This is not that. OPM's guidance to agencies is blunt about the consequence. If the only resume an applicant submits runs longer than two pages, that applicant is ineligible for further consideration. The rejection notice even has standard wording, telling you the application isn't being considered because it didn't meet the resume page requirement in the announcement. Sit with that for a second. It doesn't matter how strong your experience is. It doesn't matter that a human would have loved page three. A resume over the limit takes you out of the pool before anyone reads a word of your qualifications. Of every formatting decision in federal hiring right now, this is the one with the highest stakes, because it is the one that can end your candidacy on a mechanical count rather than the merits. The system is built to hold you to it. USAJOBS pushes you to choose a resume of two pages or less to make it searchable and to apply. You are not going to sneak a longer one through and hope a reviewer forgives it. Plan for the count. Where the rule came from You don't need the policy history to write a good resume, but a sentence of context helps it make sense. The two-page cap is one piece of a broader federal hiring-process reform. It traces to Executive Order 14170, "Reforming the Federal Hiring Process and Restoring Merit to Government Service," issued in January 2025 and published in the Federal Register on January 30, 2025. OPM's Merit Hiring Plan, dated May 29, 2025, is what actually implements the change. It prohibits the old longform federal resume structure and sets the two-page limit in its place. OPM announced implementation in a release dated September 2, 2025, a few weeks before the limit went live. The stated logic is efficiency. Reviewers were drowning in long packages, and the theory is that a shorter resume forces the most relevant experience up front and makes federal applications look more like the private sector, so people can move between the two more easily. You can agree or disagree with that. For the purposes of your next application, it doesn't matter. The rule is the rule, and this is how you work inside it. Two pages, but the content requirements didn't shrink This is the trap, and it's where good candidates lose the plot. Reading "two pages," people reach for a sleek corporate resume, a crisp summary, a few punchy lines, done. Then they get rated ineligible and can't figure out why. The cap changed the length. It did not change what a federal resume has to prove. Federal HR still rates you against the qualifications in the announcement, and it does that literally, line by line, checking whether your work history contains the specific evidence the job requires. A resume can be two clean pages and still fail if it dropped the detail that establishes you meet the grade. So the job in front of you is not "shorten." It is "compress." Keep the content that qualifies you, cut the content that doesn't, and make every remaining line pull its weight. That is a genuinely harder task than the old approach, where you could just keep typing until every base was covered. Now you have to make choices, and the wrong choices are expensive. What USAJOBS still requires in every job entry Before you cut anything, know what has to survive. For each relevant position, USAJOBS and OPM guidance still expect the same core fields that made federal resumes distinctive: Employer name and your job title. For federal positions, include the series and grade, for example GS-1102-12. Start and end dates with the month and year , like 05/2019 to 08/2022. A bare year isn't enough. Dates by month are how HR measures the length of your qualifying experience. Hours worked per week. This one is load-bearing and people cut it to save space, which is a mistake. Without your hours, HR can't confirm you have the twelve months of specialized experience the grade demands, and part-time work prorates. Even at a standard forty, you have to say forty. A description of duties and accomplishments that lines up with the announcement and addresses its required qualifications, written so a reviewer can see you can do the work at the level stated. One nuance matters here, because guidance on it is genuinely mixed. The traditional federal resume also carried a supervisor name and phone number and a salary for each job. Under the two-page cap those rank below the fields above: USAJOBS marks supervisor contact as optional, and your GS grade already signals your pay band, so a separate salary figure is largely redundant. But this is not settled the way the load-bearing fields are. Some agencies still look for supervisor information, and some announcements ask for specific details, so treat these as the first things to trim for space rather than fields you must delete, and check your announcement before you strip them entirely. References, by contrast, never belonged on a resume in the first place and always come off. How to actually fit it in two pages Here is the method that works, drawn straight from OPM's own condensing hints and from how federal reviewers actually read. Lead with the most recent and most relevant experience, and detail it fully. Your last job, and any earlier job that directly matches the announcement, gets the real estate: three to five tight, results-focused bullets each. This is where you prove the specialized experience. Don't ration it here. Compress the older and less-relevant roles. A job from twelve years ago that has nothing to do with the posting doesn't need six bullets. It might need one line: employer, title, dates. Keep that line so you don't leave an unexplained gap, but don't spend your two pages narrating it. What you did a decade ago matters far less than what you do now, and every reviewer knows it. Cut the filler that never earned its place. A generic objective statement, an unrelated early-career job, the same bullet repeated across three positions, a skills section listing things you'll cover in your experience anyway. Gone. Write in results, not narration. Reviewers scan hundreds of these. A bullet that says what you accomplished and at what scale beats a paragraph describing your daily tasks. If you're stuck turning duties into impact, our guide on showing achievement even when you don't have clean metrics is built for exactly this. One more practical point. The USAJOBS resume builder is not your friend on length. Its spacing, font, and line formatting will push you past two pages with only a handful of jobs, and a short reference list alone can eat half a page. If the builder resume looks bloated, that's the tool, not you. Many applicants draft the two-page version in a word processor with half-inch margins and a 10-point body font, then bring it over. If you'd rather start from a structure that's already tight, a clean two-page resume template saves you the layout fight entirely. Not sure your federal resume clears the two-page line? Run it through a free review to see what's dead weight and what actually proves your specialized experience, before an agency screens you out on the count. Get a free resume review → Mirror the announcement's exact language If you take one thing from this piece, take this. Federal screening is more literal than most people expect, and two pages makes precision matter more, not less. When HR rates your resume, a reviewer often works through the required qualifications one at a time and checks your work history for the matching evidence. If the announcement asks for a specific number of years doing a specific thing, they scan your bullets for that specific thing, in that specific language. Miss the phrasing and you can be rated ineligible even when you clearly have the experience, because the person screening you frequently isn't the subject-matter expert who would read between the lines. They match words. So mirror the announcement. Pull the specialized-experience statement and the key duties, and make sure your top-of-page bullets echo that language where it's honestly true of your work. This isn't keyword stuffing in the old federal sense of cramming in everything. It's the opposite. With only two pages, you spend your limited space on the terms that qualify you and drop the rest. If you're curious how automated screening reads a resume in the first place, we broke down how hiring actually works stage by stage , and it applies to federal pipelines too. What to cut first When you're a few lines over and every bullet feels essential, cut in this order. References come off first. They don't belong on a resume, federal or not, and you'll provide them when asked. Supervisor names and phone numbers go next: USAJOBS treats supervisor contact as optional and it ranks below your core experience, though a few agencies still look for it, so trim it for room and glance at the announcement first. Salary sits in the same bucket, since your GS grade already tells the reviewer your pay band. Then combine. Fold your pay plan, series, and grade into your job title line rather than listing them separately, so "Contract Specialist" becomes "Contract Specialist (GS-1102-12)" on one line. Trim any bullet that repeats across two jobs down to a single appearance under the more relevant role. Cut entire positions that don't support your case for this announcement, leaving a one-line placeholder only if dropping them would create a confusing gap. What you don't cut: hours per week, month-and-year dates, and the duty detail that proves your specialized experience. Those are the load-bearing walls. If you're tempted to thin your skills into a graphic sidebar to save room, don't; those tricks tend to break how the resume gets read. Our take on where a skills section actually belongs covers why. It's still a federal resume, not a private one The most common overcorrection is treating the two-page cap as permission to submit a private-sector resume to a federal job. It is not. The change is length, not document type. A polished corporate one-pager , the kind you'd send a startup, will often fail a federal qualification screen because it leaves out the fields the rating depends on: your hours, your exact dates, your series and grade, the specialized-experience detail. You can be perfectly qualified and still rated ineligible because your resume didn't say the things federal HR is required to check. The federal resume kept its DNA; it just lost its length. Think of it this way. You are writing a federal resume with all its required precision, then squeezing it into the space a private-sector resume uses. Both disciplines at once. That's the actual assignment, and it's why a thoughtful two-page federal resume is harder to write than either of the things it's caught between. The CV and medical-research exception There is a real carve-out, and if it applies to you it changes the whole calculation. For positions that require a curriculum vitae, typically in medical and research fields, agencies may ask you to submit your CV, with the specific information required, as an "other document."A physician's publication list or a scientist's grant history genuinely can't compress to two pages, and the rule accounts for that through the CV path rather than the two-page resume. Some announcements outside Title 5, along with certain judicial and legislative-branch postings, can also accept a longer resume if the announcement includes instructions for submitting it. And in the early rollout, some agencies and specific hiring authorities handled the transition on their own timelines. The safe move is the same one federal applicants have always needed: read the announcement. The "How to Apply" and "Required Documents" sections tell you the page requirement and any exception for that specific job. Don't assume the general rule when the announcement is sitting right there telling you the specific one. Coming from the military A large share of federal applicants come out of the military, and the two-page cap lands hard on them, because a full career of assignments, deployments, schools, awards, and collateral duties does not want to fit in two pages. The discipline is the same one you'd use anyway, now under a firm ceiling: translate, then condense. Turn your MOS, AFSC, or rating and your rank into plain civilian language a reviewer recognizes, keep the assignments that map to the announcement's specialized experience, and let your SF-50s carry the formal record of what your resume can only summarize. Our full walkthrough on translating military experience into a civilian resume gets into the specifics; think of this two-page rule as the container that work now has to fit inside. Translation is what gets a civilian reviewer to understand what you did, and condensing is what gets the whole thing under the ceiling, so you're doing both jobs at once. What to do right now If you're going to apply for a federal job in the near future, don't wait until you've found the perfect posting to deal with this. Do the housekeeping now. Open your USAJOBS profile and look at the resume stored there. If it's a leftover longform version from a previous job hunt, it's over the limit and it needs to come down to two pages before you apply to anything. If you had a searchable resume in the Agency Talent Portal, it was pulled and won't resurface until you post a compliant one. Check every version the system might hold: the profile resume, any file you uploaded, the builder resume, the searchable one. Then build your tailored two-page version around a specific announcement rather than in the abstract, because the announcement tells you which experience to lead with. Keep your old long master resume saved offline as a reference so you're not rewriting your history from scratch each time; you just pull from it and trim to fit. Before you submit, one honest read against the announcement's required qualifications, top to bottom, to make sure the two pages still prove you're qualified. If you want a second set of eyes on whether it does, that's what a review is for. Frequently Asked Questions When did the USAJOBS two-page resume limit start? September 27, 2025. That's the date USAJOBS began restricting resumes to two pages across profiles, uploads, builder resumes, and the Agency Talent Portal, per OPM's guidance. It sits under the Merit Hiring Plan issued May 29, 2025. Policy can shift, so if you're reading this well after 2026, confirm the current rule on USAJOBS before you rely on it. What happens if my federal resume is over two pages? You're rated ineligible for that job. OPM's guidance says if the only resume an applicant submits is longer than two pages, that applicant is out of consideration, and the rejection notice cites the page requirement. It isn't trimmed to fit or read anyway. The count knocks you out before your qualifications get looked at, which is why this is the highest-stakes formatting rule in federal hiring right now. Does the limit apply to the USAJOBS resume builder too? Yes. The cap covers builder resumes, uploaded files, the resume in your profile, and searchable resumes in the Agency Talent Portal. The catch is that the builder's own spacing and fonts run long, so a few jobs can push you past two pages on their own. If your builder resume looks bloated, that's the formatting, not your experience. Draft tight, then check the page count before you make it searchable. Do I still need to list hours worked per week? Yes, and don't cut it to save space. Hours are how federal HR verifies you have the twelve months of specialized experience a grade requires. Part-time work prorates, so even at a standard forty you have to write forty. Drop the hours and a reviewer can't confirm your qualifying time, which can sink an otherwise strong resume. It's one of the fields that has to survive the trim. Can I just submit my regular private-sector resume instead? No. The change is length, not document type. A polished corporate one-pager usually leaves out the fields federal rating depends on: hours, exact month-and-year dates, series and grade, specialized-experience detail. You can be fully qualified and still rated ineligible because the resume didn't say what HR is required to check. Write a federal resume with all its precision, then compress it into two pages. What should I cut first to get under two pages? References first; they don't belong on any resume and you'll give them when asked. Then supervisor contact and salary, which are lower priority and usually trimmable for space since your GS grade already implies your pay, though it's worth a check against your announcement first. Then compress older, unrelated jobs to a single line. Keep hours, month-and-year dates, and the duty detail that proves your specialized experience. Those are the walls you don't knock down. Are supervisor contact and salary still required? Guidance is mixed, so treat them as lower priority rather than mandatory. USAJOBS marks supervisor contact as optional, and your GS grade already signals your pay band, so both are among the first things to trim when you're over two pages. That said, some agencies still look for supervisor info and some announcements ask for specific fields, so read your announcement before you strip them. The fields you never cut are hours per week, month-and-year dates, and the duty detail that proves your experience. Are there any exceptions to the two-page rule? A few. Positions that require a CV, typically in medical and research fields, can submit the CV as an "other document." Some non-Title 5, judicial, and legislative-branch postings can accept a longer resume if the announcement gives instructions. The way to know is to read the specific announcement; its "How to Apply" and "Required Documents" sections state the page requirement and any exception for that job. How do I fit twenty years of experience into two pages? Prioritize. Give your most recent and most relevant roles real detail, three to five results-focused bullets that prove the specialized experience. Compress older or off-target jobs to a line so there's no unexplained gap. Cut objectives, repeated bullets, and unrelated positions. Mirror the announcement's exact language in your top bullets. The goal isn't to shrink everything evenly; it's to spend your two pages on what qualifies you. I already have a resume saved in USAJOBS. Do I need to fix it? Probably, yes. The limit reaches your stored profile resume, not just what you submit at apply time. A leftover longform resume from a past search is over the cap and needs to come down to two pages before you apply again. If you had a searchable resume in the Agency Talent Portal, it was removed and won't return until you post a compliant one. Check every version the system holds.
